It reflects our residents' priorities, the challenges we face, and the opportunities we choose to pursue. Today's proposed budget continues the work we've been doing together since 2019, building a safer, stronger, and more resilient Tampa while preparing responsibly for the future. Before looking ahead, it's worth reflecting on how far we've come. Since 2019, the City Of Tampa has made historic investment in the foundations of our community. We've rebuilt roads, expanded sidewalks, made our streets safer, and continued making meaningful steps in advancing transit options. We modernized water, wastewater, stormwater systems and completed major upgrades to our waste-to-energy plant. We've invested in Parks and Recreation, strengthened neighborhood services, expanded youth programming, enhanced homelessness initiatives like Tampa hope and continued improving public safety. I'm excited to announce that since setting a goal of planting 30,000 trees by 2030, we've already planted more than 18,000 trees in neighborhoods, parks, and public facilities all across our city. Tampa has added 23,000 homes with more than 8,300 affordable units completed or underway. We've invested over a hundred million in affordable housing, maximizing every available federal dollar and fighting for every unit. Projects like the marquee, rome yard, west river and north downtown, which will have more than 2,300 workforce and affordable homes, provide workers with affordable housing options closer to their jobs. Down payment assistance, housing rehabilitation, and renovation programs are helping residents remain in the homes they already have. Because housing stability isn't only about building new units. It's about helping people stay in the neighborhoods their families call home. These investments have helped make Tampa one of america's most desirable places to live, work, and raise a family. And none of this happened by accident. It happened because this council made responsible decisions. Our employees delivered exceptional work every day, and we remain committed to investing in both today's needs and tomorrow's opportunities. That discipline, innovation, and productivity have put Tampa on the strong financial footing that made this progress possible. Tampa isn't just growing. It's thriving. Our city continues to enjoy outstanding credit ratings, reflecting years of responsible budgeting, disciplined financial management and long-term Planning. Those ratings reduce borrowing costs, saving taxpayers millions while allowing us to invest more in critical infrastructure. We balanced our budgets, maintained healthy reserves, met our long-term obligations, and kept our debt burden relatively low compared with many peer cities. Tampa's population has grown by more than 70,000 people since 2007, yet we have fewer employees today than we did two decades ago, and fewer than comparable cities across Tampa Bay and Florida. Those aren't simply accounting achievements. They demonstrate that Tampa has managed growth responsibly while preserving the flexibility to respond to changing economic conditions. Strong finances aren't the goal themselves. They are what allow us to deliver excellent public services while protecting taxpayers. And although Tampa's economy remains strong, the cost of providing public services has changed dramatically since 2019. Our city is grappling with inflation, just like families and businesses throughout our community. An infrastructure project that costs 10 million to build in 2016 can cost more than 31 million today. The cost of asphalt has risen 50% since 2017. Concrete as much as 70%. And stormwater pipes 90%. At the same time, Tampa Bay has experienced one of the strongest periods of household income growth in our history. According to the American Community Survey, median household income in the City Of Tampa increased 56% from 2019 to 2024. More than it did in the previous two decades combined. Simply put, everything costs more and maintaining the same level of service is considerably more expensive than it was seven years ago. For much of the last decade, Tampa experienced record-setting growth, more than 23,000 new housing units and tremendous job creation. Today, the market has shifted from exceptionally hot to more normal, not declining, but stabilizing. As we prepare this budget, we're also facing significant economic uncertainty driven by inflation and in particular amendment 3, which would fundamentally change how cities across Florida fund local government. If approved by 60% of Voters, we estimate a revenue reduction of 35 to 40 million in the 2028 budget and 60 to 65 million the following year. Property taxes fund our Police Officers, firefighters and paramedics, but don't even cover the full cost of those services. Amendment 3 would create a significant funding shortfall. Protecting public safety will always remain our highest priority. I want to be clear. This amendment does not protect public safety; it threatens it. Without another long-term funding solution, the city would face difficult decisions regarding staffing and service levels, including public safety. The impact would extend well beyond emergency response. Street resurfacing, stormwater improvements, affordable house, parks, trees, litter removal, youth programming, homelessness initiatives like Tampa hope, and investments that keep neighborhoods clean, safe, and vibrant all rely substantially on the same funding source. Good financial management isn't about waiting for uncertainty to become a crisis. It's about preparing before it does. Developing a city budget begins more than 15 months before it comes to City Council. While our fiscal year 2027 budget isn't directly affected by amendment 3, it includes prudent steps to prepare for the possibility that it passes. For several years, we've invested general fund revenues in resurfacing neighborhood streets, building affordable housing, upgrading parks, and renovating fire stations. Because of the uncertainty created by the proposed amendment, this budget shifts those funds into reserves to provide a better financial buffer should it pass. It also places a hold on creating new positions. We want to continue moving forward with the important projects and quality of life investments our residents are asking for every day, but until Voters decide the future of this amendment, we cannot responsibly commit those additional resources. Good news is that this decision can be revisited after November's election. If Voters reject the amendment, we can put those important neighborhood projects and services back in the budget. Our theme is "built to last" because that's exactly what this budget is designed to do -- strengthen Tampa's foundation and ensure our city remains one of america's most exciting and livable places for generations to come. This budget continues investing in the services residents rely on every day while preserving the financial strength that has positioned Tampa for long-term success. It reflects careful stewardship of taxpayer dollars, continued investment in infrastructure and public safety, and responsible preparation for an uncertain fiscal environment. Tampa has overcome significant challenges before by Planning ahead, making disciplined decisions and staying focused on the people we serve. This budget follows that same approach. I want to thank the members of City Council, our department directors, and finance team and every city employee for their dedication to serving our residents and helping make Tampa one of the best cities in america. I look forward to working with council over the coming weeks as we review this proposed budget together and continue building a stronger Tampa for generations to come. And now I'D like to introduce our chief financial officer Dennis Rogero who will provide a detailed overview of the proposed budget.

segments.speaker: Dennis Rogero
segments.text: Thank you, council. Dennis Rogero, once again, chief financial officer. If I can have my presentation up. I want to ensure you all can see it.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Good to go. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Dennis Rogero
segments.text: You see the agenda. Again, referendum amendment 3, the referendum in November. It is the elephant in the room. We might as well talk about it. We'll dive pretty deep into that and then roll into fiscal year 2027 recommended operating and capital budget as we always do, go into detail on the capital improvement program. Again, that is the five-year plan for our capital projects. Closely linked, we'll give you insight into our existing and future debt program, and then discuss some of the nuances that have now been added to adopting the millage rate. All right. Amendment 3, so what's it do? As you heard the mayor say, the bottom line, up front, it reduces the money we're going to get and what we can do with that money. It's going to restrict us not only monetarily but in flexibility that the mayor and City Council have to use the funding. You see right here, first it triples the existing homestead exemption from $50,000 to $150,000 in fiscal year 2028. Next year, fiscal year 2029, it quintuples that same exemption to a quarter of a million dollars. $250,000. That's fivefold increase. To give you an example, our current taxation is about $19 billion for homesteaded properties in the city in fiscal year 2029 this will eliminate almost half of that. Almost half of our homesteaded properties will now be off the tax roll if this comes to pass. Obviously, that is a significant adverse impact to our future revenue. What else does it do? It further restricts our use, as I said, of that property tax funding to what you see here, basically public safety, police, fire, roads, bridges, stormwater, natural resources, flood control, retirement benefits. But, as you heard the mayor say, what this doesn't mean is that it protects these services by any means. It simply says that the property taxes we get can only be spent on these services. As you know, and we'll show in just a moment, even our current property tax revenues are insufficient to fund just our police and fire services. We will be put in a very difficult position, and we're part of a big club, many, many localities in the state will be put in a very difficult position. Cut budgets, cut positions, cut services, I don't know. Time will tell. These will be future mayor and future City Council decisions, because fiscal year '28 impacts. What it also doesn't mean, however, and I want to point this out, it also doesn't mean these services are going to be able to keep pace with inflation. Costs are going up. I don't need to tell anybody that. The services won't be able to keep pace with performance pay increases for outstanding functions of the job. They won't be able to keep pace with retirement benefits. We'll have to spend property tax funding on retirement benefits but retirement benefits historically go up. The cost of those things go up. This will not guarantee that those keep pace. What does it leave out? Turns out it leaves out quite a bit. Parks and Recreation, for one. As you heard the mayor say, about $74 million next year. Community related services. Again, as the mayor stated. Go out of My Way to mention the behind-the-scenes services that make the 49th largest city in america and $2 billion budget run as well as it does. My shop, for instance. Purchasing, human resources, technology and innovation, contract administration. We have billions and billions and billions of assets to look after and this does not fund facilities management. So how will these be funded in the future if amendment 3 passes? Well, in a perfect world, our other General Fund revenue sources would pick up the weight. I think that's highly unlikely that other revenue sources are going to be able to pick up this. State-shared revenue, charges for services, local option sales taxes, et cetera. So we'll have to come up with other revenue sources. Other localities have more than one millage, for example. Municipal service taxing units. Municipal service benefit units. Assessments for services. Efficiencies can always be looked for, but in my opinion, this is a tight organization. Can I almost guarantee you that no efficiencies are going to make up for this revenue shortfall. What will you do or what will future administrations and city councils do? Likely cut services. This is the final part of it. It simply provides funding for County Officers and Commissioners. I believe the initial draft left these out. Again, full disclosure. The County Officers and Commissioners are covered. This is a good segue into what our property taxes do and don't cover. We see this every year because every year it doesn't change. Again, property taxes don't even cover our entirety of public safety services. And those are on the left. You see that, about three-quarters of that $430 million covered by property taxes after we give our component the 62 plus million dollars to the Community Redevelopment Agencies. Right off the bat, if no changes happen on amendment 3, we're a hundred million dollars short just funding police and fire. As we add the next largest department near and dear to our hearts, Parks and Recreation, we just dig ourselves further into the hole, about $170 million short. What's that look like on a year-to-year basis? The mayor mentioned the first couple of years, for a five-year period, that coincides nicely with the capital improvement plan, we lose anywhere from 300 to 320 million dollars. Those are our estimates. As an example, give you a sense of scale, that more -- more than wipes out all of the General Fund capital improvement projects we had planned. And you'll recall over half of that was just fire. Tampa Fire Rescue. That's gone. As the mayor intro'd, this is the world we prepared this budget in. Sustaining operations. We've done that, but with an eye toward pausing, reflecting, and if necessary, adapting to a much more hostile world from a local government revenue perspective, preparing for uncertainty. That's what we're doing. In summary, we won't be able to do a great deal of what we planned on doing, whether it's capital improvement projects or operating expenses, service levels of the community. It's sobering. And i'm sure we'll talk much more about it in the days and weeks to come. Having said that, we'll move into the recommended fiscal year '27 budget. And here it is, the net fiscal year 2027 budget for all funds is just over $2 billion. About 2% more than the current year. Increases primarily due to higher compensation and benefits, including health care costs, software licensing. Again, an increase in what we are going to be compelled to give to the CRAs, the community redevelopment areas, and, of course, inflation. You see here our breakout of the major funds as we do every year and the two largest components as always are the enterprise funds and the General Fund. About three-quarters of our entire budget, and we'll get into those in more detail as we do. Then your special revenue funds, those are construction services, housing. Your trust and agency funds. Those are your CRAs and streetcar, for example. Our internal service funds, that's Fleet Maintenance and insurance. Our debt service funds, what we set aside every year to pay our debt obligations and capital project fund. Those are transfers into special funds so we can execute our C.I.P. Project. Diving deeper into the General Fund and the enterprise fund, on the left, you've got the General Fund, as we stated you've got public safety at over 60%. That's police, fire, and we include Code Enforcement in that particular slice. Then central government. Those are the functions I talked about before, the support agencies that you typically don't see on the front line, but they keep the wheels of government moving. I'll repeat them again. Technology and innovation, Revenue and Finance, human resources, neighborhood and community affairs, contract administration. Our Parks and Recreation department, again, a little over 74 million next year. Public Works -- excuse me, that's facilities and contract administration and the Public Works. And economic -- pardon me -- development. On the right at a little over $866 million, those are our enterprise agencies. Again, those are the departments that run like a business. They are enterprising, right? They have to turn what in the private sector would be a profit and reinvest those profits into their own operations. Every dollar we get for those services we can only spend on those services. They are run like a business. Got water, wastewater, Solid Waste. Those are the big ones. Parking. Parking is doing very well and it is being run like a business. Continuing with the General Fund, here is our General Fund balance history and future estimates. As the mayor stated, this plays a very, very large part in how we're preparing for amendment 3 and the rough future that may lie ahead and ITs impact. First, once again, and as always, we have a very, very good history. Picture tells a thousand words and you see it right here. I want to thank council. I want to thank the mayor for continuing to make this a very, very high priority. It's a cornerstone of our conservative financial management philosophy. You know that, and it's paying off. It continues to pay off. On the far right, you see in case amendment 3 passes in November, we are buttressing our fund balance to a level of 25% or about $190 million. You can see that's far more than our recent history of 23%. And taking out the federal aid associated with the covid pandemic, far more than our 23 to 24 percent. That's how we are amassing the funding to deal with some very, very tough decisions that we may have to make. I think it goes without saying that if amendment 3 passes, we are highly unlikely to maintain this consistency in our unassigned fund balance. We'll talk about debt and our credit ratings a little bit later. But significantly impacting in a Very Negative Way our largest and most stable revenue source is also not likely to be viewed very well by the Credit Rating Agencies. Again, we're in a big club. Almost every locality in the state is and are going to have to deal with these issues. As we do every year, we break out the General Fund further, and you see the slide here with the major changes associated with the revenues. First and foremost, of course, property taxes. They are going up a little under $17 million. We'll take it. I've seen it not go up. But I do want to point out, it's about half of what the increase was last year and significantly less than the increases of just a few years ago. This represents a 4% increase in taxable value. Last year, it was over 7%. So you've got this continuing downward trend of increases. And a downward trend of increases, I get it, it sounds odd, but again, these revenues have to keep pace with an upward trend of expenses associated largely with inflation. Sales tax down over $4 million, reflects a moderate economic slowdown and some important sales tax categories. Just need to pick up the paper to see a slow down in various sectors of the economy throughout the united states. Nice bright spot, getting back on a nice three percentage increase for franchise fees and utility taxes associated with growth. So we'll take that. Miscellaneous revenues, going down, we're expecting a little less FEMA funding than our initial estimates. Again, these are from the storms of two years ago. The FEMA wheel turns and we're happy it turns, but it doesn't always turn fast. Pilot and pilof, payment in lieu of taxes and payments in lieu of franchise fees. What we do is we charge those departments who run like a business as if they were a business. For taxes and their use of rights-of-way, the franchise fees. Those are going up almost 3 million. So we'll take that. And we've got a settlement associated with the hobbs case bringing up the bottom at $2.5 Million. Just to reiterate, about $22.4 Million revenue increases. And this is what I wanted to contrast it with. The $11 million at the bottom of major increases. So you see a good deal more revenue than what we're appropriating in the budget for expenditures. Again, that's by design. We'll detail those major increases right here. Salary and benefit increases at nearly $25 million. As we've said before, we continue to be in a very competitive environment for talent. So recruiting, retaining, and rewarding our employees remains very, very important. CRA contributions we've mentioned. Decreases in operating costs. In the past, we showed you increases in operating costs and what those increases are funding. Not this year. Not this year. A decrease in the TECO streetcar subsidy. A nice increase in the HART route one, but that's being funded by the Parking Department. Bottom line, what you've got is a very limited but a continuation of services budget. Hold the line, see what happens in amendment 3. You see we are actually reducing our positions slightly overall, two down. One up in the water, one down in construction services and two down in parking. For the first time in two decades, our total position count now exceeds the high water mark prior to the great financial crisis. It has taken us 20 years to get the number of positions we had in fiscal year 2007. Expanding on our position history, you see here our increases since fiscal year 2019 overwhelmingly in the public safety, utilities, and transportation areas. And continuing with the position theme, if you will, you see our ratio of employees to population continues to decline. And remains the lowest in our comparison group of the cities at the bottom. We're the dark blue. And continuing with the comparison theme, the mayor's recommended millage remains the same. And you see that is also less than our comparative group of cities. Jumping to the capital improvement now, quite a change from the current year capital improvement program on the General Fund part and we'll get into detail on that. But starting from a 50,000-foot view, you see the fiscal year '27, about 46 -- i'm sorry. I've got to put my glasses on. $346.7 Million. Over that five-year period, over $1.1 Billion. Overwhelmingly you see in the Wastewater and Water Department as we continue the pipes program. Here are the major projects in fiscal year 2027 that are getting additional appropriations. Again, pipes, and you see the list here, very successful program. We anticipate it's going to continue to be successful, but to be successful, we are going to have to continue issuing debt. Parks and Recreation, technology and innovation, very, very lean. Again, as we put general funding into our fund balance awaiting amendment 3. Mobility, funding sources there for fiscal year 2027. Jumping into the debt program, because they are so closely aligned and many of our projects and our plans require financing in the future. I won't belabor this too much. It's very kind of the mayor to mention our credit rating increases. As always, I want to thank council also, again, you have made it a very, very high priority. We appreciate that, and I think the proof is in the pudding. You see that here. I will state, as I always do, that these are very, very important from a financial, conservative financial management philosophy and a solid financial sustainability perspective. Every single year, as i've said before, we are monitored and questioned about these ratings. I've said it before, they don't just call it a review. They call it surveillance. All three Credit Rating Agencies, they take this very, very seriously as they should. Because these ratings are a big part of decisions, either retail investors make or Industrial Investors make when borrowing money and giving us money and funding our projects. They want to make sure we are on a very strong and solid financial foundation. And this proves that we are. I do want to highlight the issuer credit rating at the top. As we've said before and for the public's benefit, this is our equivalent of our fico score. Your personal fico score, good to great. This is absolutely outstanding, triple a for fitch and standard & poor's. On the right are the highest you can get. Moody's is the second highest. We'll keep working on that. Quite a headwind if amendment 3 passes, but, again, our individual ratings are also very, very good. I'll highlight the water and sewer bonds. The best you can get across the board with all three Credit Rating Agencies. Absolutely fantastic. I think we're only one of three in Florida, maybe one of seven nationwide. That's very, very thin air. Again, we always want City Council entering into the debt discussion with eyes wide open. These are our potential future debt issuance plans. We'll start with non-ad valorem debt. This is debt that is pledged from the General Fund but not property taxes. That's why it's called non-ad valorem. We pledge General Fund. We have no obligation to raise property taxes to pay it, but we have pledged the General Fund. It is substantially less than our previous plan. Again, because of what may happen with amendment three, a little under $80 million. With some federal grant funding in there. You're going to see throughout the timing to be determined based on project schedules and/or spend-down requirements. We always want to avoid borrowing money sooner than we need to because we don't want to pay interest on money that's not working for us. Water and wastewater debt, as I mentioned before, the continuation of the pipes program, almost $785 million. I believe council has been briefed on that third bullet point under water and wastewater, the extraterritorial rate adjustment. Speaking of headwinds, that's going to be a headwind. Quite simply, that was a 25% charge to non-municipality customers. That's going away. We'll have to deal with that. Solid Waste debt, as we discussed before, Solid Waste Department and the waste-to-energy facility have undergone a significant amount of work. Again, very successful, but we are going to roll up our existing short-term debt instruments into one large bond in 2028. And you see that there, about 250 odd million dollars. Zeroing in on our non-ad valorem annual debt service, you can see that after fiscal year 2029, we have a substantial amount of debt that comes off the books. That's great news. We get over that hump, and we've got a lot of savings, a lot. That is a technical term. A great deal of savings in our debt service and the opportunity to fund other things if future mayors and future city councils plan on it. That's part of the plan if amendment 3 does not pass. So that's a nice picture going from about 30 odd million to 13 million. Diving into a little more detail on that program, it is lean, as I said. We are confining the plan to only those projects that we have entered into a contract with. And you see them right there. Fire station 24. The Police Department Howard Avenue annex, the Fleet Maintenance decentralization. Guida house renovation and west riverwalk. We have gone, again, to reiterate from a plan that was about a quarter of a billion dollars, 250 plus million dollars, to less than 82 million. I do want to explain a change in adopting the millage rate. Again, council may already be aware of it, but again, full disclosure, they have amended the number of council members that are going to have to vote for the budget. In the past, a simple majority was enough to keep our millage the same. That is no longer the case. A simple majority you see here simply can vote for the rolled-back rate. Anything from the rolled-back rate up to 110% requires a supermajority. Five votes. Our millage of 6.2076, Something like that, our millage is going to fall, as you see at the bottom there, about 2.3% Higher than the rolled back. We will require five votes to continue the millage at the same level. And a reduction in that millage, of course, will have associated reductions in the recommended budget. This is the budget calendar going forward. Three workshops. The third of August, 10th of August and 17th of August, and our two public hearings September 8 and September 22. I will point out for those listening, the workshops on August 3 and August 10 are morning workshops. The police, fire, parks convention center and special events workshops -- workshop, excuse me, on August 17 is in the evening. Begins at 5:01. This is where everyone on the planet with an internet connection can find our budget. Finally, I do want to take just a moment to say thank you. Thank you, council, appreciate your interest and energy up to this point and what i'm sure will be continued interest and energy going forward. I also want to thank the mayor, of course, Chief of Staff, all of our departments, this fantastic communication, fantastic knowledge of their operations, and what it's going to take to keep those operations going. My entire Revenue and Finance staff, whether IT's budget, accounting, grants, et cetera, doing a fantastic job, and they make me look good. Thank you, Mike Perry. And your leadership. Absolutely vital to the organization. Appreciate the citizens advisory committee and what will continue to be the discussions going forward. I'm absolutely sure. Last on the list but first in our hearts, Ms. Kopesky, we appreciate all of your energy and input. We really do. Thank you. What a great addition. I'll just thank council again for what's to come. We have some headwinds, as I said. We've done hard things and done them before.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Thank you, ma'am. I wanted to salute you. We are at parris island and this is Boot Camp. You are going with vigor.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: It was a short agenda. We were prepared.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Still, just saying. Two quick motions. My first one is this is for October 15. I want Mr. Shelby or whoever the person would be to brief us. I'm obviously resigning at midnight on November 2. I would like a briefing on the following points, which is for my appointment on replacing, how long the process will take after my resignation and the process that will occur on this for Tampa City Council. I do this because I want to make sure while i'm still here that i'm briefed on this publicly and for the community for the public for District 7, because District 7 needs somebody here. I just want to make sure that we mitigate that time as much as possible.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Council Member, what is the effective date of your resignation?

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: November 2.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: If it's anything similar to mine, it was a two-week process. And then we had a special call, the Tuesday of the third week. Now, it may be that, but that's actually a really good point because that's been a question we've heard a lot. Would you like the clerk to come forward?

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Like before --

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: I prepared something for council, and I have it in front of me for the March 14, 2022, district 3 vacancy. It has a summary of the applicable provisions of the charter and a timeline.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Would you like to just brief us very quickly and then -- actually, yeah. Why don't we have Mr. Shelby update it --

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Bring it October 15.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: When do you want it to come back?

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: This is a briefing on the substance of what will occur.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: This is a briefing on the process of what happens. There are time constraints. The appointment must be -- the vacancies must be filled by appointment within 30 days from the time the vacancy exists. It's a very compressed timeline. The sooner you know.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Okay. October 15 it is.

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: I'll second that.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Council member Carlson.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Could you include -- I think it's important to figure out how to fill the seat quickly. Even two weeks we might lose a bunch of votes. I have a question since this time we know for sure when he's leaving, is it possible to do the vote before so we could fill?

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: You cannot fill a vacancy that doesn't exist.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Two weeks is what was given to make sure people had the time to apply.

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: Could we do October 1st? Make it a couple of weeks earlier.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: I think earlier is better to be honest. We could do September 17. That is also open.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: For the record, better say what year.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: We have a motion to have that come forward on October 1st from Councilman Viera. Second from Councilman Maniscalco. All those in favor? Aye. Any opposed? Anything else.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: Yes, ma'am. This is something I think applicable for the administration update for next week. Probably three minutes, which is we heard from the gentleman today on the k-bar cut-thru that there is a possibility they can open it like really soon for Tampa Fire Rescue, all that I really care about. I'D like whether Chief Bennett or whoever during administration update, by the way, while I was here I typed out a memo already gone out to them on this, but to brief us on the feasibility of that. This will save response times.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Motion from Councilman Viera to add the conversation about k-bar ranch cut-thru to the administrative update for next week on August 6, 2026. We have a second from Councilman Maniscalco. All those in favor? Aye. Any opposed? Council Member Carlson.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Just a quick trivia thing. Parris island, do you know the significance of parris island in Florida history?

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: No. You're "out-guidoing" me.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: On parris island, inside the military facility is the remnants of a dig site of a Spanish Settlement. The Spanish Settlement was called Santa Elena, and it was the first capital of Florida because the spanish were trying to move up to prevent the french. Outside the gates is a museum that Michael Francis from USF wrote the narrative for the museum. Anybody going near parris island, go to the museum and you'll learn about Florida history.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Excellent. No motions? I don't have anything. Mr. Shelby?

segments.speaker: Martin Shelby
segments.text: No thank you.

segments.speaker: Luis Viera
segments.text: I'm not saying this to start a conversation, but I have read with interest your negotiations with the rays, including on the East Tampa CRA and downtown and just looking forward to hearing more on that because I think those are prospectively good ideas, aside from the rays, not to open up a conversation, what I know, right.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: I have a motion to receive and file from --

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: One real quick thing. I was talking I think Bonnie wise this morning. I said I don't want to be in the center of this issue. I want to be like guido. If somebody else would like to step up and engage in the conversation, but they have offered to meet with each of us to ask what our constituents' concerns are.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: I have a motion to receive and file from Councilman Maniscalco. I have a second from Councilman Miranda. All those in favor? Aye. We are adjourned.
